text: Student visa holders may work a limited number of paid hours per fortnight while their course is in session, and unlimited hours during scheduled course breaks. The exact fortnightly limit is set by the Department of Home Affairs and has changed several times, so the current figure must be read from the official student visa page rather than from forums, agents or older guides. Working more than the limit can put the visa at risk.

section_heading: Work that does not count towards the limit
text: Some work does not count towards the fortnightly limit. Work that is a registered part of the student's course, such as a compulsory placement or practicum, is treated differently from ordinary paid employment. Volunteer work for a non-profit organisation may also sit outside the limit when it is genuinely unpaid and would not otherwise be done by a paid worker. Students should confirm their own situation against the official conditions.

section_heading: What Overseas Student Health Cover is
text: Overseas Student Health Cover, usually shortened to OSHC, is health insurance that student visa holders are normally required to hold for the full length of their visa. It helps cover the cost of seeing a doctor, some hospital treatment and some prescription medicines. Cover must be arranged before the visa starts and kept active without a gap. A small number of students are exempt under specific government arrangements.

section_heading: Using your health cover in Melbourne
text: To use Overseas Student Health Cover, a student books an appointment with a general practitioner, pays at the clinic or shows the membership card where the clinic bills the insurer directly, and then claims any eligible amount back through the insurer's app or website. Not every service is covered, and dental, optical and ambulance cover often sit outside a basic policy. The insurer's own member portal lists what a given policy covers.

Myki is the reusable card used for trains, trams and buses across Melbourne and much of Victoria. A card can be bought at staffed stations, at many convenience stores and online, and it is topped up with money or with a pass for a period of travel. A card must be touched on at the start of a trip, and touched off on trains and buses so that the correct fare is charged.

Some students are eligible for concession fares, but eligibility depends on the type of course and the student's visa. Many international students studying at a university are not eligible for the standard Victorian concession card, while some are eligible for a specific travel pass instead. Because the rules differ by institution and course, eligibility should be checked on the transport authority's concession page and with the university's student services team.

A bond is a security deposit that a renter pays at the start of a tenancy in Victoria. The rental provider must lodge the bond with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority rather than keep it in a personal account, and the renter should receive confirmation that it has been lodged. The bond is held for the length of the tenancy and is not the same as rent paid in advance.

At the end of a tenancy the bond is returned to the renter unless there is an agreed deduction, for example for unpaid rent or damage beyond fair wear and tear. Both parties can apply to have the bond repaid, and a disagreement can be taken to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal. Photographs taken at the start and end of a tenancy, together with the condition report, are the evidence that usually settles a dispute.
